1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: A 69-year-old female patient was admitted to our hospital on Day 0, with the chief complaint of "recurrent cough for 9 months, worsening with dyspnea for half a month." Nine months before admission, the patient developed cough without an obvious precipitating factor, but without obvious sputum production, and without chills, rigors, fever, hemoptysis, chest pain, weight loss, dyspnea, or other manifestations; there was no arthralgia, alopecia, oral ulcers, or rash. A chest radiograph at a local tertiary hospital showed "pulmonary infection," and no specific treatment was given. During this period, the patient had recurrent dry cough, more obvious at night and in the early morning. Two months before admission, the cough became frequent, and she received intravenous infusion therapy at a local county hospital, but without obvious improvement. Half a month before admission, the cough worsened again, accompanied by chest pressure and exertional dyspnea, without paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea or orthopnea. A chest radiograph at a local tertiary hospital showed "bilateral pulmonary infection, possible small right pleural effusion," and chest CT showed "right pleural effusion." No treatment was given, and the dyspnea gradually worsened; at the time of admission, dyspnea occurred with activities of daily living. Further history revealed that more than 11 years earlier, the patient had been diagnosed with coronary artery disease and had undergone placement of one coronary stent. She had been regularly taking aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, and other medications as an outpatient, but had stopped them on her own during the past year. During the course of the illness, there was no chest pain, chest tightness, or precordial discomfort. Three months earlier, the patient developed bilateral lower extremity edema, and intermittent edema persisted after diuretic infusion. There was no history of amiodarone use. She had been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus 1 year earlier and was regularly using insulin aspart; both fasting and postprandial blood glucose were at target. History of sulfonamide allergy. Otherwise unremarkable. The patient denied any history of smoking or alcohol use. She denied exposure to radioactive substances or chemical toxins. She denied a history of eating raw crab, fish, or shrimp. Family history was unremarkable. Physical examination on admission showed: T: 36.5℃, P: 110 beats/min, R: 21 breaths/min, BP: 143/94 mmHg, weight: 70 kg, height: 154 cm. Perioral radial furrows. No enlarged superficial lymph nodes were palpable. Dullness to percussion over the right lower lung, decreased breath sounds in the right lung, and no moist rales or crackles heard in either lung. Cardiac dullness was not enlarged, heart rate 110 beats/min, regular rhythm, accentuated P2, murmur (-). Abdominal examination was negative. No rash, mild pitting edema of both lower extremities, no joint tenderness, and skin sclerosis of the second finger joints of both hands. Pre-admission ancillary examinations were as follows: complete blood count (Day -2): WBC 8.15×10^9/L, Hb 115 g/L, N 81.5%. BNP (Day -2): 219 pg/ml. Chest radiograph (Day -2): bilateral pulmonary infection; small right pleural effusion. Echocardiography (Day -2): normal size of all cardiac chambers; localized tricuspid regurgitation, increased regurgitant pressure gradient, suggesting pulmonary hypertension; impaired left ventricular diastolic function.

differential_diagnoses.name: Systemic sclerosis-related pulmonary involvement (possible interstitial lung disease with pulmonary arterial hypertension)
supporting_evidence: Physical examination showed perioral radial furrowing and skin sclerosis of the second phalanges of the fingers on both hands, supporting a connective tissue disease phenotype, especially systemic sclerosis.
Recurrent dry cough for 9 months and progressively worsening exertional dyspnea over the past half month, consistent with common manifestations of systemic sclerosis-related pulmonary involvement
Color Doppler echocardiography showed localized tricuspid regurgitation and an increased regurgitant pressure gradient, suggesting pulmonary hypertension.
On physical examination, accentuated P2, supporting elevated pulmonary artery pressure

Chest radiograph suggested a small right pleural effusion, and chest CT showed a right pleural effusion, which may be seen in connective tissue disease-related serosal involvement or pulmonary circulation involvement
No moist rales or crackles were heard in either lung, suggesting that this is not a typical presentation of acute infectious pulmonary consolidation.
opposing_evidence: Phase 1 information did not provide a clear description of interstitial changes on high-resolution chest CT
The patient denies joint pain, alopecia, oral ulcers, rash, and other manifestations of connective tissue disease.
In the first-stage information, immunologic evidence such as autoantibodies was not provided.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary arterial hypertension with right heart dysfunction (may be secondary to connective tissue disease or other causes)
supporting_evidence: Dyspnea on exertion that began within the past half month and progressively worsened; at the time of admission, dyspnea occurred with activities of daily living.
Echocardiography showed an increased tricuspid regurgitation pressure gradient, suggestive of pulmonary hypertension.
On physical examination, accentuated P2 is a supportive sign of pulmonary hypertension
Bilateral lower extremity edema developed 3 months ago. Physical examination showed mild pitting edema of both lower extremities, suggesting increased right heart load or venous congestion.
A right pleural effusion can be seen in pleural effusions associated with pulmonary hypertension or right heart dysfunction.
opposing_evidence: Echocardiography showed that the cardiac chambers were normal in size, with no clear stronger supportive evidence such as right ventricular enlargement.
BNP 219 pg/ml is only moderately elevated and cannot by itself confirm overt heart failure
The stage 1 information did not provide a complete examination basis for etiologic clues of pulmonary hypertension.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pleural effusion and dyspnea caused by congestive heart failure/coronary heart disease-related cardiac dysfunction
supporting_evidence: More than 11 years ago, he was diagnosed with coronary heart disease and underwent coronary stent implantation, and he has self-discontinued aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, and other medications over the past year, with a risk of cardiovascular events and worsening cardiac function.
Half a month before admission, the patient developed a squeezing sensation in the chest and exertional dyspnea; bilateral lower extremity edema had appeared 3 months earlier and recurred repeatedly.
BNP 219 pg/ml is elevated, supporting increased cardiac load
Echocardiography showed impaired left ventricular diastolic function, which may cause symptoms of heart failure
Right pleural effusion may be caused by heart failure
opposing_evidence: During the course of the illness, the patient had no chest pain, chest tightness, or precordial discomfort.
No paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea or orthopnea
Color Doppler echocardiography showed that the size of each cardiac chamber was normal, with no evidence of significant systolic dysfunction.
Pleural effusion predominantly on the right side, not the typical presentation of bilateral symmetric pleural effusions caused by heart failure

differential_diagnoses.name: Infectious pneumonia with reactive pleural effusion
supporting_evidence: Two chest radiographs at an outside hospital suggested "bilateral pulmonary infection"
The patient has recurrent cough; symptoms have worsened over the past half month and are accompanied by dyspnea.
On the complete blood count, the neutrophil percentage was 81.5%, providing some support for infection.
opposing_evidence: The disease course has lasted 9 months and is characterized predominantly by recurrent dry cough, which is inconsistent with the natural course of most acute bacterial pneumonias.
No chills, rigors, fever, hemoptysis, chest pain, or other systemic toxic symptoms of infection
WBC 8.15×10^9/L is not elevated
No moist rales or crackles were heard in either lung
After infusion therapy, the cough did not improve significantly.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary embolism or chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
supporting_evidence: Dyspnea has worsened significantly over the past half month, mainly after activity
Heart rate 110 beats/min, tachycardia present
A crushing sensation in the chest can be seen in pulmonary vascular events.
Echocardiography suggests pulmonary hypertension; physical examination shows accentuated P2.
A right pleural effusion can be seen in a pleural reaction associated with pulmonary embolism.
opposing_evidence: The phase 1 information did not provide typical manifestations of pulmonary embolism such as sudden chest pain, hemoptysis, and syncope.
The phase 1 information did not provide definite thrombotic risk factors such as prolonged bed rest, surgery, tumor, or venous thrombosis.
The clinical course began with recurrent dry cough for 9 months, which is not consistent with the typical initial presentation of acute pulmonary embolism.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pleural effusion-associated malignancy (such as lung cancer or pleural metastasis)
supporting_evidence: In an elderly woman with chronic cough for 9 months, progressive dyspnea, and right pleural effusion, the possibility of a neoplastic process should be considered.
Imaging at an outside hospital suggested "bilateral lung infection"; some tumors may present as infection-like opacities or post-obstructive changes
Mild anemia (Hb 115 g/L), although nonspecific, may be seen in chronic disease or malignancy.
opposing_evidence: No smoking history
No common accompanying symptoms of malignancy such as weight loss, fever, hemoptysis, or chest pain.
No palpable enlargement of superficial lymph nodes
The first-stage information did not provide definite imaging evidence of a space-occupying lesion, nodule, hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy, etc.

Color Doppler ultrasound of the bilateral lower extremity veins

stage2_input.text: Pleural fluid routine: red and turbid, protein (Rivalta) positive 2+ P, total cell count 104200 *10^6/L, nucleated cell count 2200.0 *10^6/L, mononuclear cells 89%, polymorphonuclear cells 11%. Pleural fluid biochemistry: total protein 50 g/L (serum total protein 68 g/L), albumin 27 g/L, LDH 1960 U/L (serum LDH 4484 U/L), ADA 16.5 U/L. Pleural fluid cancer panel: carbohydrate antigen 19-9 3.7 U/ml, cytokeratin 19 fragment 115.9 ng/ml, ferritin 6335 ng/ml, carcinoembryonic antigen 3.6 ng/ml, alpha-fetoprotein 2.3 ng/ml. Pleural fluid exfoliative cytology: no cancer cells found. Pleural fluid acid-fast bacilli: no acid-fast bacilli found. Pleural fluid culture: pleural fluid bacteria negative; both rapid mycobacterial culture and Lowenstein-Jensen culture were negative. Pleural fluid antinuclear antibody panel: positive +(1:320), anti-SSA antibody +, anti-Scl-70 antibody positive +. CBC: WBC 8.61 ×10^9/L, N 81.5%; CRP 39.30 mg/L; PCT, G test, GM test, BNP, myocardial injury markers, hepatitis B serology, pre-transfusion testing, liver and kidney function, electrolytes, coagulation profile, and blood glucose showed no obvious abnormalities; urine protein qualitative + -P, urine occult blood (-); five serum lung cancer tumor markers were not elevated. Autoimmunity-related tests: serum antinuclear antibody panel: positive +(1:320 speckled pattern), anti-Scl-70 antibody positive; rheumatoid factor, CCP, anti-keratin antibody (-); complement C3, C4 (-); ANCA, anticardiolipin antibody, muscle enzyme panel, and lupus anticoagulant all (-); ESR 29 mm/h. Contrast-enhanced chest CT (Day +6): multiple patchy opacities, honeycomb opacities, and nodular opacities in both lungs, with slight thickening of the tracheal and bronchial walls in both lungs, considered inflammation; reexamination recommended after treatment. Large right pleural effusion. Compressive atelectasis of the right middle and lower lobes. Multiple calcified lymph nodes in the mediastinum and bilateral hila. Calcification of the thoracic aorta and bilateral coronary arteries. Ascites. CTPA: no obvious opacification of the right lower lobe pulmonary artery; poor opacification of the left lower lobe pulmonary artery. No obvious filling defects in the remaining pulmonary arteries. Abdominal Doppler ultrasound: 1. Cystic space-occupying lesion in the liver (cyst). 2. Gallstones. 3. Ascites. Venous Doppler ultrasound of both lower extremities: thrombosis in the proximal left superficial femoral vein and intramuscular calf veins. Echocardiography (Day +6): 1. Right ventricular enlargement with right ventricular hypertrophy (right ventricular end-diastolic diameter 23 mm, right ventricular anterior wall thickness 9 mm). 2. Severe pulmonary hypertension (PASP 67.9 mmHg) with moderate tricuspid regurgitation. ECG: ST-T changes. PFT: severe restrictive ventilatory dysfunction; residual volume function and diffusing capacity could not be measured due to insufficient lung volume. Arterial blood gas analysis (without oxygen inhalation): pH 7.430, PCO2 31.1 mmHg, PO2 63 mmHg. Bronchoscopy showed hyperemia and edema of the bronchial mucosa of the bilateral lobar and segmental bronchi; no cancer cells or acid-fast bacilli were found in the aspirate or lavage fluid. BALF differential cell count: lymphocyte percentage 71%, neutrophils 22.6%, macrophage percentage 6.4%. On further questioning, the patient had dry mouth, swallowing discomfort, and Raynaud phenomenon.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Further complete tumor-related antigen testing and whole-body PET-CT for whole-body screening
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is a 69-year-old woman with a long-standing dry cough, progressively worsening dyspnea over the past half month, and a large right-sided hemorrhagic pleural effusion, ascites, and lower extremity venous thrombosis. Although she previously had manifestations related to systemic sclerosis and was positive for anti-Scl-70 antibody, hemorrhagic pleural effusion is rare in systemic sclerosis, and the large volume of pleural effusion, accompanied by polyserous effusions and VTE, suggests that connective tissue disease alone cannot explain the condition; an occult malignancy, especially a gynecologic malignancy, must be strongly suspected. Previous pleural fluid exfoliative cytology, bronchoscopy cytology, and serum lung cancer tumor markers did not establish a pulmonary primary tumor. Therefore, further testing of tumor-associated antigens was intended to look for clues to extrapulmonary, especially abdominopelvic, tumors, to help determine the tumor origin and likelihood of malignancy, and to provide a basis for subsequent selection of the key screening direction for PET-CT, gynecologic tissue sampling, and oncology consultation.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Further complete tumor-related antigen testing and whole-body PET-CT for whole-body screening
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Clinically, the patient is characterized by advanced age, a prolonged disease course, hemorrhagic pleural effusion with ascites, right compressive atelectasis, pleural thickening, and venous thrombosis. Although infection, TB, isolated pulmonary embolism, and isolated heart failure all lack sufficient support, a definite primary lesion has still not been directly identified by routine chest CT, pleural fluid cytology, or airway sampling, and there is a high likelihood of an occult malignant tumor. The core purpose of whole-body PET-CT is to screen the entire body for a primary lesion and metastatic lesions, determine whether there are extrathoracic lesions such as in the pelvis/retroperitoneum/omentum, and explain the common cause of the pleural and peritoneal effusions and hypercoagulable state; at the same time, to distinguish whether the patchy opacities and nodular opacities in the lungs are more suggestive of inflammation or tumor metastases, thereby resolving the key clinical questions of whether malignant polyserous cavity effusions are present, where the primary site is, and what the stage is, and directly affecting whether to transfer to gynecology/oncology for further tissue sampling and treatment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Posterior vaginal fornix puncture was performed
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: After elevation of tumor-associated antigens and PET-CT indicating a large pelvic mass with omental and mesenteric nodules and retroperitoneal lymph node metastases, the likelihood of a malignant gynecologic tumor, especially an adnexal tumor, increased significantly. The patient also had pleural and ascitic effusions, dyspnea, and pulmonary hypertension, and her overall condition was poor, so a relatively direct, less invasive sampling method that could obtain pathologic clues as soon as possible was needed. Posterior vaginal fornix puncture can obtain pelvic/peritoneal effusion or lesion-related specimens to address whether tumor cells have already exfoliated and whether a pelvic malignant tumor origin is supported; the results would help, on the basis of the imaging findings, to further establish the neoplastic nature of the serous cavity effusion, narrow the range of the primary site of origin, and provide evidence for subsequent tumor staging assessment and treatment pathway selection.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Exfoliative cytology showed: cancer cells identified (possible adenocarcinoma)
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Although repeated prior pleural effusion exfoliative cytology and bronchoscopy-related cytology did not identify malignant cells, the patient continued clinically to have bloody pleural effusion and ascites, and PET-CT indicated a malignant pelvic mass and signs of peritoneal metastasis; therefore, exfoliative cytologic examination of the newly obtained posterior vaginal fornix puncture specimen was required to look for direct malignant evidence. The purpose of this examination was to determine whether tumor cells were present in the serous cavity or pelvic-related specimen and to make a preliminary assessment of the cell type, such as adenocarcinoma tendency, thereby resolving the key diagnostic question of 'whether this truly represents a malignant effusion and whether it supports a gynecologic primary malignant tumor.' The result is very important for excluding pure connective tissue disease-related serositis, infectious or thrombotic effusion, and directly affects the final diagnostic classification, the direction of oncology consultation, and subsequent antitumor treatment decision-making.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Hemorrhagic pleural effusion is rare in systemic sclerosis. In patients with concomitant connective tissue disease, hemorrhagic pleural effusion, and VTE, underlying malignant disease should be strongly considered. Further tumor-associated antigen testing and whole-body PET-CT were completed for systemic screening. The results indicated: cancer antigen 125: 564.22 ↑Ku/L (reference value <35 Ku/L), cancer antigen 15-3: 77.19 Ku/L (reference value <35 Ku/L). Whole-body PET-CT: 1. A large space-occupying lesion in the pelvis with increased metabolic activity (SUVmax 12.4), suspicious for a malignant tumor of adnexal origin. 2. Multiple nodules in the omentum and mesentery with increased metabolic activity, suspicious for metastases. 3. Retroperitoneal para-aortic lymph nodes with increased metabolic activity, suspicious for metastases. 4. Patchy high-density opacities with nodular shadows in both lungs, more pronounced in the right upper lobe, with mildly increased metabolic activity, suspicious for inflammatory lesions; follow-up reexamination after treatment is recommended. 5. Subpleural calcified foci in the apical segment of the right upper lobe, the apicoposterior segment of the left upper lobe, and the anteromedial basal segment of the left lower lobe; bilateral pleural thickening with pleural effusion, more marked on the right. 6. Hepatic cyst; ascites and pelvic effusion. Culdocentesis was performed, and exfoliative cytology indicated: malignant cells identified (possible adenocarcinoma). After oncology consultation, the tumor was considered most likely of ovarian origin.

8.final_diagnosis_and_diagnostic_basis.final_diagnosis: Gynecologic tumor (malignancy of probable ovarian origin) and CTD-ILD (systemic sclerosis likely associated with the tumor), systemic sclerosis?
diagnostic_basis: Elevated cancer antigen 125 and cancer antigen 15-3

Whole-body PET-CT showed a large pelvic space-occupying lesion with increased metabolic activity, suspicious for a malignant tumor of adnexal origin; multiple nodules in the omentum and mesentery, and metastases to retroperitoneal para-aortic lymph nodes
Cancer cells identified on exfoliative cytology of posterior vaginal fornix puncture (possible adenocarcinoma)
Dyspnea improved after oral corticosteroids and compound cyclophosphamide; improved with antirheumatic treatment.

treatment_plan: Methylprednisolone/prednisone tablets (40 mg qd, gradually tapered slowly)
Compound cyclophosphamide tablets 100 mg qd (long-term oral administration without dose reduction)
Low-molecular-weight heparin for anticoagulation + Maizhiling for edema reduction
treatment_response: Follow-up chest CT showed a decrease in pulmonary lesions, and the pleural effusion gradually decreased to near-complete resolution
